As discussed in the Objective 2 report, OTEC relies upon key marine resources to be technically and economically viable. Below is a brief summary of these conclusions: 1. OTEC needs to be located in an area with a suitable water temperature gradient to make the Rankine cycle sustainable (Kilcher, Fogarty and Lawson 2021). A 20 °C difference between the shallow layer warm water and deep layer cold water is often quoted as a requirement for an efficient OTEC system (Sadoughipour, Tang and VanZwieten 2025 3 OESI 2.0 M-1 T-1-P1.1 – Objective 3 Report April 2025 [forthcoming]). In the GOA, this can typically be achieved in deep-water areas (>1,000 ft), although in the warmer months this difference can occur in shallow waters, too, due to warmer surface temperatures. 2. Studies have also shown that proximity to the Loop Current is essential to ensure continued “renewal” of the cold-water supply in the GOA. 3. The OTEC equipment that the seawater flows through must be installed no higher than 30 feet above sea level, and preferably below sea level (the reasoning for this is documented extensively in the Objective 2 report), precluding topsides installation on most GOA structures. 4. Finally, due to the prohibitive costs of power transmission in the GOA, the proximity of OTEC power generating plant’s location to the intended end-use is crucial. Given these limitations and the availability of these resources in the GOA for OTEC, it is clear that the possible OTEC locations will be far from the majority of the current plugged and permanently abandoned (PA) wells which are mostly clustered in shallower waters. This means that for OTEC to power well monitoring, it will need to work via a battery charging and swapping scheme. Furthermore, the passive monitoring systems identified in Objective 1 of this study tend to be designed with multiple-year battery spans—aiming to be truly passive once installed. Therefore, the monitoring portion of this study focused on powering AUVs with OTEC, which can hypothetically perform periodic monitoring via optimized routes. The approach and results are discussed in [reference to the OTC paper]. Because of OTEC’s documented inherent economies of scale, larger plants would produce electricity at a lower cost. Whereas megawatt-scale power capacity far outweighs the demand for monitoring alone, it could be used to supply a certain portion of an oil and gas platform’s power demand.
